goal: Unplugged: name the parts of a device with their right words, sort them as input or output, and meet the system-diagram (input part, computer box, output part, with arrows).
note: Anchor: the teacher presses one key and a letter appears on the class screen; what happened in between? Opens with a three-minute retrieval of grade 1 part names (name four pictured parts, then sort them). Words taught: input, output, keyboard, screen, speaker, work together. Practice IC3. Base: Connecting computers (Year 3) lessons 1 and 2, adapted. Leans on the archived Teach Computing Curriculum (2023), not yet loaded in the source store (later.csv L149): placed from lesson titles, provisional; credit once in the day. Standards: 2026 CSTA PK-12 Computer Science Standards (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

goal: Device: pairs trace one action from input to output (a key press to a letter on the screen, a button press to a short tone) and lay it on the system-diagram, saying how the parts work together.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): predict what the screen will show after one press, then press and compare. About 12 minutes at the device; driver and navigator switch at the halfway signal (IC5). No microphone or voice input. Tools: any school device with a text box and a Curio Class page with a button that plays a short tone. Paper path: a pictured press-to-screen chain laid on the system-diagram mat. Device day, written four ways (one device per pair, 15 for 30; a few devices at stations with the other pairs on the paper version; one screen with a child at the device for each step; no device). Devices carried with two hands, cords behind the table; the last four minutes put devices away. Base: Connecting computers lesson 2, adapted. Leans on the archived Teach Computing Curriculum (2023), not yet loaded in the source store (later.csv L149): placed from lesson titles, provisional; credit once in the day.

goal: Unplugged: fill the benefit-risk-chart for one pictured tool: how it helps, how it can hurt, and what a person could do about the harm; then each child explains one new action card (a press, the part, what changes) to the teacher, about 6 minutes, fifteen children.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): one story card about a shared device, right way or wrong way. Pictured tools only (a video call with a grandparent, a drawing tool, a game). Sensitivity: no child is asked what devices are at home or how long they use screens; screen-time harms are told as feelings anyone can have, never a family failing. Spoken E2-SYS-HW-11 look-for (how the parts work together for a new, unseen action) heard from fifteen children during partner work, about 6 minutes. Practice ESR1. Candidate kept: the base's "how do devices help us" lesson as the helps column, zero added days. Base: Connecting computers lesson 3, adapted. Leans on the archived Teach Computing Curriculum (2023), not yet loaded in the source store (later.csv L149): placed from lesson titles, provisional; credit once in the day.

goal: Unplugged: on a paper pretend page, see that what is posted or sent is seen by real people and can be kept and passed on; sort kind and unkind messages and a picture shared without asking, say what happens next, and place it on the chart; then each of the other fifteen children explains one new action card (a press, the part, what changes) to the teacher, about 6 minutes.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): share or keep private, three cards. One card is a classmate's picture posted as your own, so crediting others' work is named (ESR2). Sensitivity: online safety; no real name, photo or message is said or written; the teacher page carries health's "If a student tells you something" steps word for word. Spoken E2-SYS-HW-11 look-for heard from the other fifteen children during partner work, about 6 minutes. Our own (no base lesson). Standards: 2026 CSTA PK-12 Computer Science Standards (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

goal: End-of-unit assessment: sort new part cards and place a new action on the system-diagram; one benefit and one harm of a new pictured tool and what to do about the harm; spoken, what happens next to a new pretend-page post and to whom.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): split a pictured task into two parts. Unseen items. Sequenced, not run at once: first the paper items, read aloud to the whole class together, about 10 minutes, collected from every child; then the one spoken item (E2-SYS-SE-12) heard in five groups of six, about 20 seconds a child and 3 minutes a group (about 15 minutes), while the rest of the class does a quiet unscored picture task (draw your own step-card, or color the next unit's anchor card). With the retrieval that is 28 of 30 minutes, so the retrieval stays only while the paper part keeps to 10 minutes. E2-SYS-HW-11's spoken part comes from days 3 and 4. Response time: day 6.

goal: Respond: reteach the missed parts of unit 1 by error letter and give each missed item again in a new form.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): one shared-device rule card. Groups by error letter; the teacher marks the class checklist by exception.

goal: Unplugged trace: follow a worked step-card dance with a start card (when the bell rings), a sequence and a repeat card that holds the steps it repeats, then dance it and see how the repeat makes the cards shorter.
note: Anchor: the teacher's eight-card dance of the same clap and stomp, and the class looks for a shorter way. Retrieval (3 minutes): split a pictured task into parts on step-cards. Words taught: repeat, loop (two meanings), event, when, algorithm, times. Practice CT6. Dance moves done in place (clap, stomp, turn, wave), never a spin with eyes closed; any move may be done seated or with hands only. Math bridge: equal groups come in math grade 2 unit 8 (weeks 27 to 29), so the repeat count stays at 2 to 4 and is counted pass by pass on fingers or a tally, never as a total. Our own (no base lesson). Standards: 2026 CSTA PK-12 Computer Science Standards (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

goal: Modify: change the repeat count, the start card or one step of the working dance, predict what will be different, and check by dancing it.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): sort a new part card as input or output (unit 1). Practice of day 7's cards only; one change at a time, predicted with "I predict it will ___ because ___". goal: Make: each pair writes its own step-card algorithm with one start card, a sequence and one repeat, for a dance or a drawing (draw a square: forward, turn, repeat 4), and another pair follows it and says whether it worked.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): a pretend-page card, what happens next (unit 1). Practices CT8 and IC3. Candidate kept: the drawing algorithm (a square) beside the dance for children who cannot do a move, zero added days. This algorithm becomes the pair's unit 3 program (keep the cards). Unit 2's end-of-unit assessment is the mid-year check on day 11. Product look-for, by exception and unscored (no assess mark), used by day 12: it has a start card; the repeat holds the steps that repeat; it was tried by the other pair and changed when it went wrong. Dance moves in place. Math bridge: equal groups come in math grade 2 unit 8 (weeks 27 to 29), so the repeat count stays at 2 to 4 and is counted pass by pass on fingers or a tally, never as a total.

goal: Unplugged: play a classroom rule as written (who is line leader, a tag-free game only the fastest runner can win) and judge with three tests whether it is fair: an equal chance, anyone left out, could one child win every time.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): swap two steps of a game card and say what changes. Practice ESR1. Short read-aloud of a class that changes how it picks a helper. Sensitivity: the fast-runner rule touches disability; talk stays on the rule, never on a classmate who is slower or uses a wheelchair; the teacher picks the game so no child is singled out, in the wording the sensitivity read settles from the NCDJ guide. Judging only; designing a fairer rule is not asked. Our own (no base lesson).

goal: Unplugged: compare number data and word data, how each is collected (measure, count, ask, look) and what each tells, put both in a two-column paper data-table beside a picture-graph of the same data, and make simple comparisons.

goal: Unplugged: turn a vague question into one data can answer (which game does our class pick most for indoor recess), set aside a question data cannot answer well (which game is the best one), and refine a pair's own question from a picture prompt.

goal: Unplugged society day: case cards of the counting frame (abacus) of China and Japan, the knotted-cord records (khipu) of the Andes and the raised-dot reading code made by Louis Braille, placed on a timeline strip; children say what problem each solved or what idea it helped people record or share, and for whom.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): place two cards on the timeline, before and after. Each case card is a span, not a point: from the earliest use its source documents to today where the source says it is still used, never an invention date or one people's tool replacing another's. Abacus: used for centuries in China and Japan and still common today (the Computer History Museum page gives no origin date; opened 2026-11-26), drawn as the longest span; khipu: the Inka period and earlier Andean peoples, as the Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian page words it (403 on 2026-11-26, a browser check for the lead); braille: from the 1820s to today (Library of Congress page). Braille (reading and writing) and khipu (records) carry the ideas part of E2-SOC-HI-14, the abacus the problem part. Teacher source line (publisher, period, date opened): Computer History Museum abacus page; Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian Inka khipu page; Library of Congress Louis Braille exhibit. Two views with one dated source each. Sensitivity: Native and disability content; khipu told as the record-keeping of the Inca and other Andean peoples and part of Andean life today where sources say so, never a lost mystery; braille told as a tool a blind teenager made for blind readers; no child acts blind or wears a blindfold; wording from the sensitivity read and its starting pack (the NFB braille page is a "browser check"). Our own (no base lesson).
